views.reason: Both offenses grade well (UNC success rate #16, UConn rushing EPA #9) and both defenses are below average, especially UNC's run defense (#144) against UConn's ground game and UConn's pass defense (#160) against Mensah. UNC's slow pace (9.85 drives) offsets UConn's faster tempo (11.54), so I project about 10.5 drives each and roughly 2.9 points per drive. UNC's recent games have gone over the total. Home field of about 2.5 points plus a mild motivation edge for UConn nearly cancels UNC's better efficiency, which makes this close to a coin flip.

Florida State has the better offense (0.19 EPA/play, 3.05 points per drive) against a Boston College defense that is solid, especially against the pass. Boston College's passing offense is weak (-0.07 EPA/play) and it just lost 47-2 at Duke, so it relies on the run. FSU's defense is poor against the pass, which gives Boston College some scoring room. I project FSU slightly ahead after a 3-point home-field adjustment for Boston College. FSU's 12-game road losing streak and its coaching turmoil keep this close and the confidence low.

Both defenses rank near the top nationally (Texas allows 0.78 points per drive, Missouri 0.93), and both offenses are only average to good, so scoring should be limited. Missouri's passing offense is better, but Texas's pass defense is elite and Texas has injuries at skill positions and tackle. Missouri plays faster (about 12.7 drives to Texas's 11.5), and with home field I project a narrow Missouri edge in a game of roughly 11-12 drives per team.

Both defenses rank in the top 40 in points per drive allowed, and UCLA's pass defense is elite (#3 in EPA allowed) against a weak Minnesota offense (#174 in EPA/play). UCLA's offense is only average, and the backup QB, Ty Dieffenbach, lowers its ceiling. UCLA's rushing edge should be enough for a narrow road win after about 2-3 points of home field for Minnesota. Pace is moderate at roughly 12 drives per team, so the total should be low, around 36.

Baylor's defense is elite (top 15 in EPA allowed against both the pass and the run, 1.08 points per drive allowed), and Iowa State's offense has been inconsistent on the road, scoring 10 at BYU and 3 at Arizona. Baylor's offense is about even with Iowa State's, and its defense is much better, so it should score on the weak Iowa State run defense. Baylor also gets home field and a possible interim-coach boost. Iowa State's passing game should still get some points, though. The pace is moderate, around 12 drives a side, which puts the total in the low 50s.

Tulsa has the better offense, with a strong rushing game (#26 in EPA) against a Tulane run defense ranked #154. Tulane's offense is weak (#207 in success rate) but faces a mediocre Tulsa pass defense, and its QB situation is unclear. Both teams give up plenty in the second half of games and recent games have gone well over projections. Home field of about 2.5 points puts Tulane slightly ahead in a game with roughly 55 points total.

Utah has the better offense (#1 in success rate, #2 in rushing EPA) and a top-5 run defense. That run defense is the key against a BYU team that relies on the pass. BYU's slow pace (10.4 drives a game) trims possessions to about 21 combined. With Utah's home edge of about 3 points, I project a Utah win by roughly a touchdown with a total in the mid-50s. BYU's passing game and a good defense keep it competitive. LJ Martin being questionable is a minor negative for BYU.

Syracuse's above-average offense (3.04 points per drive) meets an elite Clemson defense, so I regress it to about 25 points with home field. Clemson's weak passing offense is offset by a fast pace and a Syracuse defense that is only average, giving roughly 22. The result is a close game with a total near 47.

Both teams average about 11 drives a game. Duke's defense is the stronger unit (1.42 points per drive allowed, top-25 in the country), but its offense is middling (3.03 points per drive, success rate 125th). NC State's passing offense (EPA/play 0.38) should find room against a Duke pass defense ranked 77th, while its own defense is below average against the run and pass. Duke's season numbers are inflated by blowouts of weak opponents, and it scored only 19-25 against its better opponents. I project NC State at home by about 4 (2-3 points of home field) and a total around 52.

Purdue's offense is well ahead of Maryland's in efficiency (EPA/play 0.24 vs 0.05, with a strong passing game), and Maryland's defense is poor against both pass and run. Maryland's offense is below average, but Purdue's defense is also weak, so Maryland should score some. Pace is slow on both sides (about 11 drives each), which holds the total near 55, and home field adds about 2.5 points for Purdue.

Auburn has the better offense (3.05 points per drive, #43, vs 2.61 for Arkansas) and the better defense (1.76 allowed per drive vs 2.04). Both teams run about 11 drives a game, so the total stays moderate at roughly 46. Arkansas has slumped lately (lost 7-34 at Texas A&M and 10-34 to Missouri), and Auburn's recent losses were to stronger teams. Home field adds about 2-3 points, which gives Auburn about a 7-8 point edge.

Oklahoma State has a top-10 offense by EPA and points per drive, and Kansas State's pass defense is mediocre (#128). The Cowboys' defense is weak (#125), but Kansas State's offense is only average, and its QB situation looks shaky: Avery Johnson is out for the season and Blake Barnett is also out. Home field is worth about 2.5 points, but I still lean Oklahoma State in a high-scoring game, with roughly 11 drives each at about 3.0 points per drive for the Cowboys and 2.7 for the Wildcats.

Georgia State's passing offense (#28 in EPA/play) and fast pace (12.3 drives a game) face an App State pass defense that grades above average, but App State has the better defense overall. Georgia State's run defense (#200) and pass defense (#172) are weak, which should let App State move the ball even though its rushing offense is poor. App State's recent offense has been erratic (3 points in each of two of its last four games against Old Dominion and Georgia Southern), but home field of about 2-3 points and the defensive edge give the Mountaineers a narrow lead. Combined drive count is about 24 at roughly 2.4 points per drive, so I project a total near 56.

South Carolina's offense (3.81 points per drive, strong passing and rushing EPA, Sellers at QB) faces a Texas A&M defense that ranks well against both pass and run, so I expect it to score below its season average. Texas A&M's offense is mediocre, especially through the air, and it has scored 20 or fewer in four of its last five games against FBS opponents, while South Carolina's defense is only average. With home field worth about 2-3 points, I project South Carolina by a touchdown in a game of roughly 11 drives per side and a total near 49.

Delaware has the better offense (EPA 0.21 vs 0.07) and faces a Kennesaw defense that is only average, while its own defense is poor, ranking near the bottom against both the run and the pass. Kennesaw's offense is mediocre, but it has been scoring recently and Delaware's defense should give up enough. Expect roughly 11.6 drives each at about 2.4 points per drive, with home field (2-3 points) narrowing the gap to a near pick'em that leans slightly to Delaware.

Arkansas State has the better offense (#25 in success rate, 2.78 points per drive) against a UL Monroe defense that allows 3.0 points per drive and ranks #196 against the run. UL Monroe's offense is weak (1.61 points per drive), but Arkansas State's defense is poor too, so the Warhawks should get a couple of scores. Arkansas State plays slowly (10.1 drives a game), which caps the total in the mid-50s. Home field and the bye week push the margin to about 15.

LSU is better on both sides of the ball by efficiency: points per drive of 3.86 against 0.94 allowed, with the #1 defense by EPA. Alabama's offense is elite by EPA, but it has scored 10 and 17 against good defenses and now faces the best pass defense in the country. Alabama's run defense is strong and LSU's rushing is only average, so I expect about 11 drives each with moderate scoring. LSU gets about 3 points for home field, and Alabama is thin on injuries.

Houston has the better offense (#2 in success rate, 3.72 points per drive) and the better defense (1.42 points per drive allowed) against a Cincinnati defense that ranks in the bottom half of the country against the pass. Houston also plays slowly (about 10 drives a game), which caps the total, but its efficiency should still produce several scoring drives. Cincinnati's rushing offense (#4 EPA) will score some, but Houston's solid run defense and home field (about 3 points) point to a Houston win by about 11.

UAB is the better team on both sides of the ball, with a top-20 pass defense that should exploit Charlotte's weak passing offense. Charlotte's defense ranks near the bottom in pass defense, so UAB should score well enough on the ground and in short fields. UAB's slow pace (10 drives a game) limits the total, and Charlotte still scores a bit thanks to UAB's mediocre run defense. About 3 points of home field are included.

Georgia Southern has the better offense (EPA/play 0.17 vs 0.10, points per drive 2.78 vs 2.20) and the better defense (1.88 points per drive allowed vs 2.19), and it gets home field. Marshall's defense is weak against both the run and the pass. Georgia Southern's slow pace (10.5 drives a game) and its recent low-scoring wins hold the total down to about 48. Marshall's bowl motivation and its good offensive success rate keep it within a touchdown.

Ohio State has the better offense (0.34 EPA/play, 3.44 points per drive) against an Oregon defense that is elite on paper (1.14 points per drive allowed), and Oregon's offense is mediocre (2.76 points per drive) against a top-15 Buckeye defense. Oregon's recent scoring has been low (15, 17, 10 in three of its last four), and Ohio State is likely to control the game at home with about 2-3 points of home field. Pace is the difference: Oregon runs a fast tempo, but a game between two strong defenses should land around 12 drives per team and a total in the low 40s.

Navy has the better offense (#19 EPA/play, #4 in passing) against a Temple defense ranked near the bottom against the pass and run, and it should score about 2.8 points per drive. Temple is a slow-paced team at 9.5 drives a game, which limits possessions on both sides. Navy's pass defense is also poor, so Temple can score some, but Navy's stronger efficiency and home field give it a clear edge. That puts the projected total in the low 50s.

Both offenses are below average in EPA and rushing, and both defenses are top-50. Penn State's pass defense (#4) should limit Washington's passing game. Washington gets home field (about 2.5 points) and a slightly faster pace, so I project about 11 drives each at roughly 2.1 to 2.3 points per drive. That gives a total in the low 40s and a narrow Washington win.

Wake Forest is a top-15 offense (3.88 points per drive) facing an FCS Merrimack defense that gave up 42 to Delaware. Merrimack's offense is among the worst in the country (0.29 success rate, rushing EPA 236th of 238), and Wake's run defense is 5th, so it should struggle to score. Wake's slow pace and a doubtful QB Gio Lopez cap the total somewhat, but the backups should still get a lot of scoring in a blowout.

Two similar, below-average teams with weak defenses, especially against the run (MTSU #214, WKU #190). MTSU has a slight edge in points per drive and home field worth about 2.5 points. Pace is moderate at about 11.4 drives each, which points to a total around 50.

Kansas has the better efficiency profile on both sides of the ball (offense EPA #39 vs #82, defense #20 vs #55), and it gets about 2.5 points of home field. Both teams run about 12 drives a game and score about 3.2 points per drive. Each defense is slightly better than average, so I project roughly 11.5 drives each at about 2.5-2.7 points per drive. UCF's 32-point loss to Baylor, a team Kansas beat by 1, and its worse results against TCU point toward Kansas, though UCF's offense can still score against a defense this size.

North Texas has a top-5 offense by EPA in both passing and rushing and plays fast at 12.1 drives a game. Rice's pass defense is weak, so North Texas should score at about 3.3 points per drive on roughly 11.5 drives. Rice's offense is one-dimensional, with a bottom-5 passing EPA and a decent run game, and it plays slowly, which caps its drives. Rice should still score some against a poor North Texas pass defense, but North Texas wins comfortably at home.

Louisiana Tech has the better offense and defense by efficiency. Its passing game (#39 in EPA/play) faces a Troy pass defense that is good (#21), but Troy's points-per-drive-allowed rank of #197 shows it leaks scores. Troy's offense is mediocre, especially through the air (#182), and Tech's top-30 run and pass defenses should hold it near 20 even with home field. Pace is slow for both teams, around 11 drives each, so I project a moderate total in the mid-40s.

San Jose State has a clear defensive edge: it is #43 in points per drive allowed, while Northern Illinois is #231 and #234 against the run. Northern Illinois's one real strength is its rushing offense, but San Jose State's run defense is solid. The Spartans' offense is poor, though, so I expect them to win with about 12 drives and roughly 2.2 points per drive against that defense. Northern Illinois is slow-paced and inefficient, so I project about 11 drives and 1.3 points per drive against the San Jose State defense. Home field adds a couple of points.

FIU's defense (#74 in points per drive allowed) is much better than Missouri State's (#215), but FIU's offense is poor (1.67 points per drive, #221) and its rushing is bottom-tier. Missouri State's offense is about average, so I expect roughly 10 drives each and about 2.2 points per drive for the Bears against FIU's defense. FIU gets a boost from home field and Missouri State's weak pass defense, which should let the Panthers score a bit more than their season average. I project a close game with FIU slightly ahead, and the Liberty blowout loss is a reason to hold the projection down.

Mississippi State has the better offense by efficiency (EPA/play 0.28 vs 0.19, points per drive 3.43 vs 2.46) and gets home field. Vanderbilt has lost five straight and allows 30 a game, but Mississippi State has scored 0, 15 and 3 in its last three against stronger opponents, so I trim its output below its season average. Both teams play at a slow-to-middling pace of about 10-11 drives, which keeps the total around 51.

Wisconsin's defense is elite (top 10 in points per drive allowed and run defense), and Rutgers is down its starting QB, a top WR and some OL. Rutgers' defense is among the worst in the country, especially against the run, which suits Wisconsin's best unit, its rushing offense. Both teams play slow (about 10-11 drives), so I project around 41 points total with Wisconsin winning by double digits at home.

Louisiana's defense (EPA/play allowed -0.03, #58) is far better than South Alabama's (#226 overall, #232 against the run), so Louisiana should score well above its 2.69 points per drive. South Alabama's passing offense (#14 in EPA/play) will find some room against a decent Louisiana pass defense, but its recent form is poor (3 losses in its last 4). I add about 2.5 points for home field and project roughly 11.4 drives per team, which puts the total near 57.

Colorado State owns one of the worst defenses in the country (0.30 EPA/play allowed, 3.30 points per drive allowed, bottom against both pass and run), and Boise State's offense is top-15 in EPA, especially on the ground. Boise's slow pace (about 10 drives a game) trims the total. Colorado State's offense is efficient enough to score 27 at home, and Boise's defense is only average, but the backup QB (Max Cutforth) adds some risk for Boise. Boise still wins comfortably.

Tennessee's defense is elite (0.92 points per drive allowed, #2, and #4 against the pass), and Kentucky's strong rushing offense faces a run defense that is only average. Kentucky plays slowly, about 10.6 drives a game against Tennessee's 11.9, which should keep the total moderate. Home field adds roughly 2.5 points for Tennessee, giving it a modest edge. Kentucky's 7-1 record came in many one-score games and its defense allows 24.8 a game, so I discount its record somewhat.

Jacksonville State has a top-35 offense by EPA and success rate against a Sam Houston offense ranked near the bottom nationally, at about 1.1 points per drive. Sam Houston's defense is decent by EPA, but it has been worn down by a bad offense, and its QB situation is shaky. Jacksonville State plays at a slow pace of under 10 drives a game, which caps the total. I project roughly 9-10 drives each, with home field adding 2-3 points to the margin.

Georgia's offense is elite (#4 success rate, #7 EPA/play) and faces an Ole Miss defense that is only average (#70 EPA allowed, with a weak pass defense), so Georgia should score consistently. Ole Miss's offense is also elite, led by the #3 rushing attack, but it is without RB1 Lacy and faces a top-5 Georgia defense. Georgia's defensive edge, plus its better health, outweighs the 2-3 point home-field advantage for Ole Miss. Pace is slightly slow for both teams, which points to a total in the high 50s.

Both teams run heavily and play at the slowest pace in the country (about 9.5 and 9.8 drives a game), but both defenses are poor against the run and the pass. Army's offense is better (3.56 points per drive against 3.27) and it has home field. I project about 10 drives each at roughly 3.3 points per drive for Army and 2.4 for Air Force, whose passing game is the worst in the country. That puts the total in the mid-50s.

Michigan has a top-35 defense, ranking in the top 30 against both the pass and the run, and Michigan State's offense is poor in EPA terms (#143) and has scored 10 or fewer in three of its last six. Michigan's offense is only average at about 2.4 points per drive, but it faces a pass defense ranked #176 and gets home field. Pace is slow, about 11 drives per team, so I project roughly 41 total points with Michigan winning by about two scores.

Miami has the nation's top offense by EPA and points per drive, but its pass defense is weak (#161). Notre Dame's offense is also elite (#2 in points per drive), and its defense is strong against the pass (#7), which blunts Miami's main strength. Both teams play at a slow pace, about 10.7 to 11 drives each, so I expect roughly 11 drives per side. I project about 2.6 points per drive for Miami against Notre Dame's defense and about 2.9 for Notre Dame against Miami's. Home field gives Notre Dame the edge, so I have the Irish winning narrowly in a total of about 58.

Arizona State has the better offense, especially on the ground (rushing EPA #18), and gets about 2.5 points of home field. Colorado's run defense is strong, but its offense is mediocre and its defense is thin on the line and at safety. Colorado is also dealing with QB uncertainty after Julian Lewis's medical emergency, and Arizona State's QB Mikey Keene is questionable. Pace is moderate at about 12 drives per team, so I project a total around 49.

Northwestern's offense is elite by efficiency (top 10), but starting QB Chiles is out and backup Marchiol is a downgrade, which pulls that number down. Iowa's defense is top-25 and its run D (#3) shuts down the Wildcats' rushing strength; Iowa's own offense is average, but Northwestern's run D is weak. With slow pace (about 10.3 and 11.1 drives) the total lands in the mid-40s, and home field makes it a near coin flip with a slight Northwestern edge.

Louisville has the top rushing offense in the country by EPA and a top-20 scoring offense, facing a Georgia Tech defense ranked near the bottom against both run and pass. Louisville should get about 2.9 points a drive over roughly 12 drives. Georgia Tech's offense is mediocre and its QB situation is unsettled, though Louisville's defense is only average and the Jackets get 2-3 points for home field, so they score in the mid-20s.

Florida's offense is far more efficient (3.87 points per drive, #5) than Oklahoma's (2.27). Oklahoma's defense is elite by EPA and points per drive allowed (1.10), which should slow Florida below its season average. Pace is about 11.5 drives per team, and with Oklahoma's offensive coaching turmoil and 2-3 points for home field, I project Florida by about 8.

Liberty is much stronger on both sides of the ball, with a top-30 offense in EPA and success rate and a top-30 defense. New Mexico State's passing offense is among the worst in the country (#223 in EPA/play) and its points per drive is 1.58. Liberty's slow pace (about 10.4 drives a game) limits the total, but at roughly 3.0 points per drive against an average defense it should still reach the mid-30s, while NMSU gets about 1.1 points per drive against Liberty's defense for roughly 12. I include about 2.5 points of home field for NMSU.

Texas Tech's top-20 defense, especially its #5 run defense, should slow a West Virginia offense that has been strong in EPA and scoring. West Virginia's pass defense ranks near the bottom (#218 in EPA allowed), so Tech can score even with only average passing numbers. Tech is at home and needs the win for playoff hopes, which supports a margin of about 14, and WVU's fast pace keeps the total in the low 60s.

Fresno State has the better offense (2.72 points per drive, against Utah State's 1.82) and has been scoring well lately. Utah State's defense is good (22nd in points per drive allowed), though its pass defense could be tested. Pace is slow, about 11 drives each, so I project roughly 20-25 even after giving Utah State home field. Utah State's offense is weak and Fresno State's defense is mediocre, so the Aggies should score in the low 20s at best.

Hawai'i has the better offense and a modest edge in the common-opponent comparison (-11 vs -54 against New Mexico, -4 vs -13 against San José State). UTEP's offense is among the worst in the country (14 ppg, 1.69 points per drive) and its defense allows 36.5 a game. Hawai'i's pass defense is bad too, so UTEP gets some scores at home. I project about 11.3 drives each, Hawai'i at roughly 2.5 points per drive and UTEP at roughly 1.8, with 2-3 points of home field for UTEP already included.

Wyoming has the slowest pace in the country (9.2 drives a game) and a weak passing offense (#214 in EPA/play), so it will struggle against UNLV's good pass defense (#46). The Cowboys' one real strength is the run game, which meets a middling UNLV run defense. UNLV is a bit better on both sides of the ball and gets about 2.5 points of home field, but its offense is only average. Wyoming's slow pace should hold the game to roughly 11 drives per team, so I project a modest total of about 43.

The two offenses are nearly identical in efficiency (EPA/play 0.21 each, points per drive 3.08 vs 3.16), and both defenses are below average, especially Texas State against the pass. Oregon State plays faster (about 12.3 drives a game), has the better scoring defense, and gets home field (about 2-3 points). That points to a high-scoring game, with Oregon State winning by about a touchdown.
